books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, B. Contention Between Whites and American Indians over Western Lands
The Jackson Presidency and Jacksonian Democracy

stimulus.text: The portrait, published in 1838, shows Sequoyah (Se-Quo-Yah), a Cherokee leader, holding a tablet covered with the characters of the Cherokee syllabary, the writing system he invented. The Cherokee used the syllabary to print their own newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, beginning in 1828.
stimulus.source_note: Portrait 'Se-Quo-Yah,' McKenney-Hall series, drawn, printed and coloured at I. T. Bowen's Lithographic Establishment, Philadelphia, published 1838 (Library of Congress). Public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The discovery of gold on Cherokee land in Georgia in the late 1820s best shows that removal was driven mainly by

options.text: white Georgians' desire for valuable land
the Cherokee's refusal to adopt American ways
options.misconception: Removal is often explained as a clash of ways of life, so it is easy to blame the Cherokee for refusing to change.

options.text: a Supreme Court order to remove the Cherokee
options.misconception: The Court is part of the removal story, so it is easy to think it ordered the removal.

options.text: the Cherokee's request to move west
options.misconception: Jackson described removal as protection, so it is easy to think the Cherokee asked for it.

rationales.A: Gold made Cherokee land suddenly precious, and Georgia's land rush turned a slow pressure for removal into an urgent demand.
rationales.B: The Cherokee had adopted American ways, as the syllabary and the Phoenix show, yet they were removed anyway.
rationales.C: The Court ruled for the Cherokee in Worcester v. Georgia in 1832; no Court order told them to leave.
rationales.D: The Cherokee resisted removal through their chief, John Ross, and in the courts; they did not ask to move.
rationales.general:
1. Date the rush. Gold was found on Cherokee land in the late 1820s, just as Georgia pressed hardest for removal.
2. Ask what gold changes. It turns farmland into a prize, and white settlers who wanted the land found a new reason to demand it.
Background: the Cherokee had a written language, a newspaper, and a republican government, so 'failure to civilize' cannot explain removal.
Remember: when a policy follows a discovery, ask who wanted what was discovered.
